articles.title: Mike Tyson earned an estimated $400 million in boxing, filed for bankruptcy in 2003; at 60, his perfume collection is worth $50,000
articles.summary: Former heavyweight boxing champion Mike Tyson earned an estimated $400 million during his career, but by 2003, he had filed for bankruptcy with reported
articles.body: Former heavyweight boxing champion Mike Tyson earned an estimated $400 million during his career, but by 2003, he had filed for bankruptcy with reported debts of $23 million. More than two decades after his financial collapse, the 60-year-old boxing legend has rebuilt his wealth through business ventures, entertainment projects, sponsorships and public appearances. Yet one luxury habit has stayed with him. In an interview with People published on October 16, 2026, Tyson revealed that he continues to spend heavily on luxury fragrances, particularly those made by Swiss perfume house AMAFFI. He estimated that his collection of fragrance bottles is worth around $50,000. The revelation comes as a new Netflix documentary revisits his extraordinary rise, extravagant lifestyle and personal struggles.Mike Tyson's $50,000 luxury perfume collectionTyson revealed his continued interest in luxury fragrances while discussing his life and spending habits in an interview with People. Asked about the luxury item on which he still spends considerable money, he named fragrances from AMAFFI, a Swiss luxury perfume house.“I have a bunch of bottles, probably worth about $50,000 total,” Tyson told the publication.The figure refers to the estimated combined value of his collection, rather than a confirmed annual spending amount or the price of a single bottle.AMAFFI is known for its elaborate perfume bottles, which incorporate decorative finishes and details featuring crystal, gold and silver plating. According to the company, crafting some fragrances can take up to two years.The brand's fragrances listed on its website range from approximately $2,000 to $6,000, according to People. At those prices, a collection of several bottles can represent a substantial luxury purchase.How Mike Tyson lost his fortune and filed for bankruptcyTyson's financial troubles became public in 2003, when he filed for Chapter 11 bankruptcy protection in the United States. At the time, he reported debts of approximately $23 million, despite having earned hundreds of millions of dollars during his boxing career.His financial collapse followed years of lavish spending, costly legal disputes, divorce settlements and problems with the management of his finances. Contemporary reports described a lifestyle that included luxury cars, mansions, expensive jewellery and exotic animals.Tyson's former lawyer said at the time that the boxer had relied on others to manage his financial affairs and had discovered that his debts far exceeded his assets.Estimates of his career earnings vary. While the recent People report puts the figure at around $400 million, reports published around his bankruptcy commonly cited approximately $300 million in ring earnings. The higher figure has also appeared in later accounts of his financial history.The distinction is important because career earnings represent money brought in over time, not the amount a person retains as wealth. Taxes, expenses, debts, legal costs and other financial obligations can substantially reduce the amount left over.The extravagant lifestyle behind Tyson's financial troublesAt the height of his fame, Tyson spent heavily on luxury possessions and an elaborate lifestyle. Reports from the period described a collection of more than 25 luxury cars, including several Bentley models, along with mansions and Bengal tigers.His financial difficulties were not attributed to spending alone. Legal disputes, divorce settlements and problems involving people responsible for managing his money also contributed to the collapse.In August 2003, the Associated Press reported that Tyson had squandered nearly $300 million in ring earnings through lavish spending and poor financial advice. His bankruptcy became one of the most prominent examples of a major sporting figure losing a fortune despite earning enormous sums during his career.The experience marked a turning point for the former heavyweight champion, who later pursued new ways to earn money outside the boxing ring.How Tyson rebuilt his wealthTyson gradually returned to public life through entertainment, business ventures, sponsorships and appearances. He took roles in films and television, developed commercial projects associated with his name and continued to attract attention through boxing-related events.In 2020, he returned to the ring for an exhibition bout against former world champion Roy Jones Jr. He later faced Jake Paul in a professional boxing match in November 2024, drawing global attention to the event.His earnings from entertainment and commercial ventures have helped him rebuild his finances, although a reliable, independently verified figure for his current net worth is not established by the People report.Tyson's fragrance collection offers a glimpse into his present-day spending habits, but its estimated value alone does not establish his overall financial position.Netflix documentary revisits Tyson's lifeThe fragrance revelation came as Tyson discussed the Netflix documentary series TYSON, which revisits his career, personal struggles and life beyond boxing.In the People interview, Tyson reflected on the difficult experiences of his past and said he was grateful for how they had shaped him. He also said he had reached a decade free from alcohol and cocaine.Despite the excesses associated with his years at the height of his fame, Tyson said his focus now is on fatherhood and looking ahead.His story spans a remarkable financial arc, from enormous boxing earnings and an extravagant lifestyle to bankruptcy and a gradual return to commercial success. The $50,000 fragrance collection is a small but striking detail in that larger story, showing that luxury remains one of his indulgences even after his financial collapse.You use AI every day. articles.summary: Amazon techie Keyul Patel shared his experience of moving back to India after working for seven years in the US.
articles.body: Amazon techie Keyul Patel shared his experience of moving back to India after working for seven years in the US. For Patel, there has been no change of company, job, or title. He is doing exactly the same job in India that he was doing in the US. But it is the work culture that made all the difference. In a blog post, Patel compared the experiences in both countries and how the same company can function differently in two countries.Patel wrote that a few things are considered defaults at a job in the US and not perks. Respect, better treatment and work timings are the three things on the top of his mind. And there are smaller comforts in the US that leave applications get auto-approved and the work-life boundary gets respected without any drama."None of this felt special while I was there. It felt normal — almost invisible. You do not wake up grateful for a predictable calendar. You assume that is just how professional life works. It is only when those things disappear that you realize how much you had taken for granted," Patel wrote.As Patel started working from India -- for the same company, in the same role, those defaults disappeared like they never existed. One technical disadvantage he cited is that meetings are scheduled for US time zones which make it past evening in India."Work hours are not defined. They stretch. They bleed. They follow whoever holds the most power on the call, not whoever is sitting in the most inconvenient time zone," he said, adding that managers schedule meetings past 6pm not as an exception but as a pattern implying that the after-work evening hours should be flexible. Even a sick leave needs approval in the system, he observed."That is the part nobody warns you about when you move back. Not one big loss — a hundred small defaults you never named, suddenly missing all at once. I am not writing this to complain about India or to romanticize the US. I am writing because it is surprising — genuinely surprising — to watch how land changes your external value. The same person. The same skills. The same employer. The same job title. Mostly the same work. Different geography, different country, different rules. The respect, the treatment, the regard for your time — it did not travel with person in their suitcase," Patel wrote.

articles.title: In 1687, Isaac Newton published the book that explained gravity, with Edmond Halley paying for its printing; after passing through a British lord's family, a first edition sold for Rs 5.49 crore in 2026
articles.summary: A book published in 1687 helped change how humanity understood the universe.
articles.body: A book published in 1687 helped change how humanity understood the universe. Written by English mathematician and physicist Isaac Newton, Philosophiae naturalis principia mathematica presented mathematical laws that explained the movement of objects on Earth and the motion of planets and other celestial bodies.Nearly 340 years later, a first edition of this historic work sold for US$576,000, approximately Rs 5.49 crore, at Christie’s on October 13, 2026. The sale drew attention not only to Newton’s scientific legacy but also to the book’s survival through centuries of ownership. The copy featured a contemporary calfskin binding, a folding engraved plate illustrating a comet’s orbit, and diagrams printed alongside the text. Its ownership history included Lord Kennet of the Dene and the late Lady Kennet, connecting the scientific landmark to a British aristocratic family.The book that changed how the universe was understoodNewton’s Principia, as the work is commonly known, was published in London in 1687. It brought together ideas about motion and gravity in a mathematical framework that helped explain phenomena that had previously been studied separately. The book set out Newton’s three laws of motion and his law of universal gravitation. Together, these principles helped explain why objects fall towards Earth, how moving bodies behave and how the movements of planets can be understood through the same underlying physical laws.Before Newton, astronomers such as Nicolaus Copernicus, Galileo Galilei and Johannes Kepler had made important contributions to understanding the heavens. Newton built on earlier discoveries and showed how mathematical principles could connect motion on Earth with the movements of celestial bodies. The achievement became one of the most influential developments in the history of science. Although modern physics has expanded and revised aspects of Newtonian theory, his laws remain important in fields such as engineering, astronomy and classical mechanics.Edmond Halley helped bring Newton’s ideas to printThe story behind the book is also one of scientific collaboration. Astronomer Edmond Halley encouraged Newton to develop and publish his work after learning about his mathematical explanations of planetary orbits. Halley did more than support the project intellectually. According to the Christie’s catalogue, he helped correct the proofs, supervised the preparation of diagrams and persuaded Newton to make the work public. He also paid the printing costs because the Royal Society, which supported the publication, had run short of funds.Newton acknowledged Halley’s contribution in the book’s preface, crediting his efforts and persistence for helping bring the work before readers. This support was crucial. Newton’s ideas might have remained less accessible without Halley’s determination to see the manuscript through publication. The episode illustrates how major scientific advances can depend not only on an individual’s discoveries but also on people who help communicate and distribute them.A rare first edition with a distinguished ownership historyThe copy sold in October 2026 was the first edition published in 1687. Its title page belonged to a version identified by a two-line imprint, a detail that helps specialists distinguish it from another issue bearing a three-line imprint and naming bookseller Samuel Smith. The book measured approximately 24.5 by 18.9 centimetres and retained its contemporary sprinkled calf binding, with the edges of its pages coloured yellow. It also contained a folding engraved plate depicting a comet’s orbit, along with woodcut and typographical diagrams.Its condition showed signs of age. The title page had a short tear that had been strengthened from the back, while the pages displayed occasional spotting and light browning. The binding had been repaired, its endpapers renewed and its corners restored. A black protective clamshell box accompanied the volume. The provenance was another notable feature. The catalogue traced the copy through an earlier owner identified as E. James, whose signature was dated 1773, and bookseller Bernard Quaritch. It later belonged to Lord Kennet of the Dene and the late Lady Kennet, who sold it at Christie’s in 2015. The current owner acquired it at that auction.Why Newton’s book remains valuable centuries laterThe Rs 5.49 crore sale reflects more than the age of a printed volume. First editions of historically important scientific works are valued for their rarity, condition, documented ownership and influence on human knowledge. Principia occupies a special place because it helped establish a mathematical approach to understanding nature. It connected the behaviour of objects on Earth with the movements of bodies in space, shaping scientific thought for generations.The book’s history also reveals the people and institutions behind its publication, from Halley’s financial support to the printers who produced the edition. Its journey through private ownership and auction rooms adds another layer to its significance. More than three centuries after its publication, Newton’s work continues to represent a turning point in science. Its sale demonstrates how an object created to communicate revolutionary ideas can become a historic artefact in its own right.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. articles.title: NI weather: Warning in place ahead of Storm Boelo
articles.summary: A Met Office weather warning is in place from 18:00 BST on Saturday until 15:00 GMT on Sunday.
articles.body:
Strong winds of up to 75mph could cause disruption across parts of Northern Ireland this weekend as Storm Boelo moves in.

A Met Office weather warning has been issued from 18:00 BST on Saturday until 15:00 GMT on Sunday.

Strong westerly winds are expected to become widespread on Saturday evening, with very windy conditions continuing overnight and through much of Sunday.

Gusts up to 60mph (96kph) are forecast widely, while coastal and exposed areas could have gusts reaching up to 75mph (120kph).

The strong winds will come with heavy, blustery showers at times.

Conditions are expected to gradually improve from the southwest during Sunday afternoon as the strongest winds begin to ease.

In light of the warning, Causeway Coast and Glens Borough Council has cancelled its fireworks display at Ballymoney on Saturday.

In statement, the council said: "We understand how disappointing this will be, but the decision has been taken with the safety of visitors, staff and event personnel as the priority."

Risk of power cuts and travel disruption

The Met Office has warned that strong winds could cause disruption to transport networks and essential services.

Power cuts are possible, which could also affect mobile phone coverage and other services.

There is a small risk of damage to buildings, including roof tiles being blown off, while flying debris could pose a danger to the public.

Road, rail, air and ferry passengers could face longer journey times or cancellations, with some roads and bridges potentially closing.

Coastal areas could be particularly vulnerable, with large waves and beach material potentially being thrown onto seafronts, coastal roads and nearby properties.

The arrival of Storm Boelo comes just a day after Storm Austen is expected to bring heavy rain and strong winds to parts of Ireland.

Storm Austen is forecast to track towards the south coast of Ireland on Thursday evening and into Friday morning, bringing the risk of flooding and travel disruption.

Irish weather service Met Éireann has issued an orange rain warning - the second highest level - for six counties in the Republic of Ireland, including Cork, Dublin, Kerry, Waterford, Wexford and Wicklow.

The Irish weather service has warned of possible flooding, public transport disruption and very difficult driving conditions.

A nationwide yellow warning for rain and wind is also in place from 19:00 on Thursday until 10:00 on Friday.

Although no weather warnings have been issued for Northern Ireland in connection with Storm Austen, widespread rain is expected on Thursday night before clearing eastwards on Friday morning.

articles.title: South of England braces for 70mph winds from Storm Austen
articles.summary: Hampshire, Dorset, the Isle of Wight, Berkshire and Oxfordshire prepare for Storm Austen.
articles.body:
Communities across the South are bracing for the impact of Storm Austen.

The first named storm of the UK's storm season is forecast to bring strong winds and heavy rain from Thursday night, according to the Met Office.

The Met Office has issued a yellow weather warning for wind for Dorset, the Isle of Wight and parts of Hampshire which comes into effect at midnight, while northern Hampshire, Berkshire and Oxfordshire will be under a warning from 10:00 BST on Friday.

Emergency services have urged people across the region to take care and avoid unnecessary risks, while ferry sailings have been cancelled and some schools and businesses have announced plans to close.

SSEN, which runs the electricity network across most of the region, has said it is entering "weather warning status" in central southern England as a result of the forecast.

People have been advised to prepare for potential power cuts as a result of the storm.

Anyone who sees any damaged electrical equipment is urged to stay back and contact the provider on 105.

Southampton, Portsmouth and the Isle of Wight are in the Met Office's southern yellow wind warning, which is between midnight and 17:00 on Friday.

Parts of Hampshire not on the coast are included in an inland yellow warning from 10:00 to 21:00 on Friday, which mentions inland gales with gusts of up to 55mph during the day.

Hampshire and Isle of Wight Fire and Rescue Service has issued advice to residents ahead of the incoming storm.

People are advised to bring loose outdoor items inside, warning that everyday objects can become "dangerous projectiles" in strong winds.

They have also encouraged the public to avoid parking under trees, keep mobile phones charged, and carry a torch in case of power cuts.

Wightlink has cancelled a number of sailings across all three of its routes on Friday, with the most severe weather expected around the middle of the day.

The operator has added an extra sailing on the Lymington to Yarmouth route on Thursday evening, departing Lymington at 22:00 and Yarmouth at 23:00, to help people travel ahead of the storm.

Customers with affected bookings are being contacted directly, the company said.

Isle of Wight Council is asking residents to avoid putting their bins out the night before collection.

The authority urged people to put their bins out in the morning and collect them promptly to avoid them blowing over and obstructing roads and paths.

Glenwood School, in Emsworth, has announced a closure on Friday, warning that the high winds pose "significant safety risks to pupils and staff".

An outdoor cinema event planning to show two horror films at Robin Hill, on the Isle of Wight, has been cancelled. The Exorcist and The Shining were set to be screened on Friday and Saturday as part of the annual Dark Woods Outdoor Cinema.

Dorset and Bournemouth, Christchurch and Poole are also in the Met Office's southern yellow wind warning.

Gusts of 50 to 60mph are likely, with 70mph or more possible on some coasts and exposed spots.

The Met Office has warned that large waves and beach material thrown onto seafronts, coastal roads and properties could cause injuries and pose a danger to life.

The RNLI, based in Poole, has encouraged people to be vigilant and avoid unnecessary risks as Storm Austen heads to Dorset.

"If you plan to visit the coast or a waterside location, we urge you stay a safe distance from the water as conditions could knock you off your feet or wash you into the sea," said water safety manager Ross Macleod.

Anyone who finds themselves in trouble in the water is advised to lie back, extend their limbs and "float to live". Those seeing others in danger are asked to "phone, float, throw": contact the coastguard, tell the struggling person to float and throw them something buoyant.

Dorset Council has warned that Portland Beach Road and the causeway may have to close temporarily overnight and into Friday morning, with a risk of flooding and waves overtopping.

The highest risk is expected between about 03:00 and 08:00, with possible disruption continuing into the morning rush hour.

People travelling to or from Portland on Friday morning have been advised to check conditions before setting off, allow extra time and make only essential journeys where possible.

Weymouth Angling Centre has told anglers that Chesil Beach, which stretches from West Bay to the Isle of Portland, is "unsafe and unfishable".

Minterne House and Gardens has announced that it will close its gardens on Friday and Saturday for safety reasons.

Reading, West Berkshire, Wokingham, Bracknell Forest, Windsor and Maidenhead and Slough have been added to a Met Office yellow wind warning, which runs from 10:00 to 21:00 on Friday.

The warning, issued on Thursday morning, says inland gales are possible, with gusts of between 45 and 55mph during the day.

The Met Office said heavy rain, combined with many trees still being in full leaf, meant some power cuts and travel disruption were possible.

People have been advised to check road conditions and bus and train timetables before setting out.

A Diwali event due to take place in Reading town centre has been moved from Saturday to 7 November as a result of the forecast. Diwali Light It Up! had planned to bring illuminated puppets, lanterns, live music and dance to Broad Street.

Oxfordshire is also covered by the inland yellow warning from 10:00 to 21:00 on Friday.

Gusts of up to 55mph are possible, and the Met Office has warned there could be short-term loss of power, with some bus and train journeys likely to take longer.

Forecasters said further spells of wind and rain were likely through the weekend and into next week, although the heaviest rain is expected further west.

Councils, including Oxfordshire County Council and South Oxfordshire District Council, have warned residents to take care and follow updates on the weather.

articles.title: Ilhan Omar says 'bizarre' pre-dawn raid on her home is forcing her to move out
articles.summary: The congresswoman said federal agents seized over a dozen items, including cell phones and notebooks, as part of a federal investigation.
articles.body:
Minnesota Representative Ilhan Omar has said she can no longer live in her Washington DC home after it was searched by federal agents last week, fearing her address has been exposed after the raid.

"With the death threats that I deal with, it's not, it's no longer going to be feasible to be in that house and have my kids," she told MS NOW .

In Omar's first public interview since the pre-dawn search of her home, she detailed how Homeland Security Investigations agents seized over a dozen items, including cell phones and notebooks, as part of an investigation.

The government has not said what crime Omar is accused of but that the raid was "part of an ongoing federal criminal investigation".

The search follows multiple comments from officials that cast doubt on Omar's US citizenship, which she received in 2000 after her arrival from Kenya.

More than a dozen subpoenas have also been issued to members of Omar's family, as part of the investigation, and it was reported that her personal computers and passport were among the items that were seized.

Recalling the hourslong raid of her home with MS NOW, Omar said: "It obviously did freak all of us out."

Omar said agents began "pounding on the doors" of her home at around 06:00 EDT (11:00 BST) on 12 October, startling her and her husband, who were both in bed.

"We were screaming," she said, as the couple ran downstairs to see what was happening, calling the incident "so bizarre".

The Minnesota Democrat estimated that between15 to 25 agents encircled her home, all of whom she said "conducted themselves in a decent way".

Agents presented Omar with a warrant at the door after she asked for one.

She then watched from the couch as agents spent roughly five hours going from room to room, Omar said, leaving with a total of 17 items, including multiple cellphones, notebooks, and her husband's camera from the 1960s.

The BBC contacted the Justice Department for comment after being referred by the DHS.

Omar again criticised the government's investigation, suggesting that it was meant to be intimidating.

Immediately following the raid last week, she posted a statement online where she called it "an outrageous abuse of power" and "weaponisation of federal law enforcement to target political enemies".

Former President Barack Obama has also blasted the federal probe, saying in a lengthy statement that it was "so appalling" .

Omar, who has represented Minnesota since 2018, has long been a target of President Donald Trump's, who has repeatedly suggested she "go back" to Somalia.

He has denied any involvement in her investigation, saying it has "nothing to do with me".

At an Ohio rally in October, Trump referred to the search of her home, saying: "I don't know what they're doing with it, but I can tell you this: she's a disaster."

The congresswoman, however, rejected the president's response, arguing that "he's got everything to do with it".

"You know, this goes back to 2019 when he was screaming about the fact that, you know, I, I need to be sent back, I need to be deported."

articles.title: Monaghan: Woman in her 70s dies after two-car collision
articles.summary: The collision happened on the N2 at Broomfield, County Monaghan, on Thursday morning.
articles.body:
A woman, aged in her 70s, has died following a two-car collision in the Republic of Ireland.

The collision happened close to the Northern Ireland border on the N2 at Broomfield, County Monaghan, on Thursday morning.

Both drivers of the cars, a woman in her 30s and man in his 50s, were transferred to Our Lady of Lourdes Hospital for treatment of serious but non-life-threatening injuries.

The road remains closed and gardaí (Irish police) are appealing to anyone who may have witnessed the collision, which occurred at about 10:10 local time, to contact them.

articles.title: Meet Lucy, who started selling plants at 8 in memory of her grandfather and raised more than £26,000 for a cancer charity
articles.summary: Lucy was 8 when she started selling plants in memory of her Grandad, Derek Easton, who died in June 2024 after 6 years of treatment at The Royal Marsden.
articles.body: Lucy was 8 when she started selling plants in memory of her Grandad, Derek Easton, who died in June 2024 after 6 years of treatment at The Royal Marsden. She wanted to thank the hospital and help other families facing cancer. Lucy began with a small wooden cabinet, plants donated by people who knew her Grandad and seeds she grew herself. In a March 2026 story titled “Lucy’s inspiring plant sale: over £24,000 raised and growing”, The Royal Marsden Cancer Charity described how her fundraising had grown since she started selling plants in 2024. An anonymous donor matched her fundraising total at Christmas, bringing it to about £24,652 at that time. As of October 21, 2026, her JustGiving page showed £26,877.46 raised, plus £540 in Gift Aid, from 83 donations. The total included £14,302.46 in online donations and £12,575 raised offline, including the anonymous matched gift. Lucy told The Royal Marsden Cancer Charity that the awareness fundraising creates for the charity matters more than the amount raised. Her story shows how a small, local initiative can grow into meaningful support for people affected by cancer.Lucy’s plant sale for The Royal Marsden Cancer Charity: how an 8-year-old began selling plants in memory of her GrandadIn her account for The Royal Marsden Cancer Charity, Lucy explained that her idea grew out of a simple wish to do something that would make people happy. “Flowers always make people smile,” she said, explaining why she decided to grow plants from seed and sell them. Over the summer of 2024, her family looked out for garden centres and people they knew who were giving plants away for free. Her mum started a Facebook page to support her, and soon people who knew her Grandad began turning up with pots and bags of plants. Within a few weeks, Lucy had enough stock to sell.She began with a small wooden cabinet, but within 2 months she needed something bigger. A local builder who was a friend of her Grandad built her a wooden stall, which is now filled with seasonal plants. Lucy says running it has been a lovely way to meet people and has helped her family cope after her Grandad died. The stall has also become a shared hobby. Her mum and her nanny, who were not previously interested in gardening, can now name lots of plants. They often spend Saturday afternoons repotting, restocking and looking for new seeds to plant. Lucy says it felt good to do something positive that could help a family like hers. The stall has taught her a lot about plants, too.Retroperitoneal liposarcoma and specialist sarcoma care: why Lucy’s Grandad’s 6 years of treatment mattered to herLucy’s Grandad, Derek Easton, died in June 2024 from retroperitoneal liposarcoma, a rare soft tissue cancer, after 6 years of treatment at The Royal Marsden. The term “retroperitoneal” refers to the area behind the abdominal lining. The review Targetable Pathways in the Treatment of Retroperitoneal Liposarcoma estimates that soft tissue sarcomas account for about 1% of adult malignancies and that retroperitoneal sarcomas make up about 20% of soft tissue sarcomas. The UK guidelines for the management of soft tissue sarcomas recommend that people with suspected soft tissue sarcoma be referred to a specialist regional service and managed by a specialist team.Lucy told The Royal Marsden Cancer Charity that the specialists at the hospital gave her Grandad nearly 6 extra years with his family, which she described as priceless. She wanted to support the hospital’s charity in recognition of the care her Grandad received. She hopes the money will help people going through similar experiences and says fundraising matters because it supports work that can improve cancer care and develop treatments. Lucy also wants more people to know that The Royal Marsden Cancer Charity supports the hospital’s work for people with cancer, rather than being limited to those who live in London. Some people she met had never heard of the charity.Charity plant stall fundraising: more than £25,000 raised, free compost, a 20-mile drive and a Christmas gift from a strangerLucy says reaching her first £1,000 was a huge moment because she could not believe how supportive her community was. Smaller acts of kindness have stayed with her, too. At a local garden centre where she went to buy compost, the owner recognised her from social media and told her it was free that day. One summer, a man drove 20 miles to find her stall. He did not come to buy anything. Instead, he brought a plant that his sister had cared for over many years. His sister had died of cancer, and he wanted to thank Lucy for what she was doing.The biggest surprise came at Christmas, when an anonymous donor matched her fundraising total, bringing it to about £24,652 at the time. Lucy says the gesture left her speechless and was the best Christmas present she could have asked for. As of October 21, 2026, her JustGiving page showed £26,877.46 raised, plus £540 in Gift Aid. Lucy plans to keep going for as long as the community supports her. Her advice to anyone thinking of fundraising is that it can be hard work, but people are often keen to buy something when they know the money is going to a charity. Those who want to support her can donate through Lucy’s JustGiving page or find other fundraising ideas on The Royal Marsden Cancer Charity’s ways to fundraise page.You use AI every day. articles.title: V Harish: YouTuber arrested after Indian finance influencer's suicide
articles.summary: V Harish, who ran the hugely popular Instagram account "Finance with Harish", was found dead on Tuesday.
articles.body:
A 27-year-old finance influencer's suicide in India has been mired in allegations of cyberbullying and started a conversation around who should give financial advice to investors.

V Harish - who ran a hugely popular Instagram account called "Finance with Harish" - was found dead on Tuesday morning at his home near Chennai, capital of the southern state of Tamil Nadu.

His suicide came just weeks after his account was disabled by Meta after complaints of irregularities.

In a complaint lodged with the police, his father J Vinayagam has alleged that his son took his life because of online harassment by Jason Samuel, a YouTuber and CEO of tech-centric venture studio Zemuria.

Police arrested Samuel on Thursday under suspicion of trying to "extort money from Harish" and posting "defamatory videos against him on social media".

BBC Tamil has not been able to reach him for comment. Earlier, he denied wrongdoing in a post on X.

The case has brought into focus the growing influence of financial content creators in India, where millions of first-time investors increasingly turn to social media for market advice.

Harish began posting videos about finance and investing around five years ago, building a substantial online following.

Over the years, he published more than 1,500 videos and amassed more than 1.3 million Instagram followers. He described himself as a financial adviser to "millionaires" and "high-net-worth individuals".

He often used music, film clips and photos of global political leaders to make dramatic videos while talking about the rise and fall of the share market and prices of gold and silver.

The videos, which broke down financial issues in simple terms, became hugely popular as they coincided with a rapid expansion in India's retail investor base, especially since the 2020 Covid-19 pandemic.

The country's largest stock exchange, the National Stock Exchange, said earlier this year it now had more than 130 million unique investors registered with it as opposed to under 30 million in 2019.

But in September, Meta took down Harish's Instagram page after receiving complaints he was not registered with Indian market regulator Securities and Exchange Board of India (Sebi) - which is required under law to be able to offer investment advice or manage client portfolios.

A back-up account, which gained over 60,000 followers in a short time, was also subsequently taken down following complaints from social media users and others.

A few other accounts in his name remain on Instagram, though with much smaller followings - and it's not clear who runs them.

According to Harish's friends and family, he recorded a video message before his death in which he said that "five years of hard work has been stolen" from him, news channel NDTV reported .

The video, which has also been shared widely on social media, shows him speaking in Tamil and then switching to English to say "I'm very sorry" to his parents, sister, friends and followers.

Police say Harish's father J Vinayagam has blamed "cyberbullying, defamatory social media posts and repeated blocking of his channels" for his son's suicide and named Jason Samuel in his complaint registered at Kanathur police station near Chennai.

Samuel had posted a video on his YouTube channel on 18 October questioning Harish's credentials since he did not have Sebi or Amfi (Association of Mutual Funds in India) registrations. In it, he mentioned that Harish's Instagram account had been disabled following complaints.

This, Vinayagam says, triggered severe online harassment and led to pressures that drove his son to take his own life.

"We demand that a proper investigation be conducted and legal action be taken against Jason Samuel and his accomplices, who spread defamation on social media and caused mental distress through cyberbullying," his complaint states.

A police statement says Vinayagam's complaint was registered under "abetment to suicide" and preliminary investigations found Samuel had a "role in this case".

"[Samuel] will be produced before court and sent to judicial custody," it says.

Samuel has defended the video in which he flagged Harish's lack of credentials saying he was acting in the consumer interest.

In a statement on X, Samuel said he was "deeply saddened, heavily grieving, shocked and frozen at what has happened and I mourn the loss of life".

He however, rejected allegations of "cyber-bullying" Harish.

"I have not cyber-bullied him. I pointed out his lack of licence and authority, misrepresentation of licence and fraud... his illegal activity.

"I literally asked him in the video to come back and do this with a proper Sebi licence. I never intended or expected this drastic measure to happen and I mourn the loss," he wrote.

If you're having thoughts of suicide, or know someone that might be, you can find support lines in India via the AASRA website or globally via Befrienders Worldwide . In the UK you can call the Samaritans Helpline on 116 123 or visit samaritans.org .

articles.title: In 2018, a Texas woman’s home was auctioned for $20,000 to pay an unrelated judgment; after years of litigation, an October 21 appeals ruling let her continue arguing it had homestead protection
articles.summary: A Texas woman whose home was auctioned for $20,000 in 2018 to recover money owed in an unrelated dispute was given another chance by the court to
articles.body: A Texas woman whose home was auctioned for $20,000 in 2018 to recover money owed in an unrelated dispute was given another chance by the court to challenge the sale on Wednesday. After years of litigation, the Texas Court of Appeals ruled that her claim deserves further examination. However, the ruling does not mean she has recovered the property.Francine Lee Lankford says the property had been her home for more than 20 years and should never have been put up for auction. According to the judgment document available on Justia, the dispute began with a small-claims judgment against Lankford in Lee County in 2017. The money she owed was not connected to the purchase of her house or any unpaid property taxes. Even so, the following year, her property at 418 Taylor Road in Elgin, Bastrop County, was put up for sale to recover the amount.The property was bought by Tracy Ortiz for $20,000 at the auction held on September 4, 2018. She was the only bidder at the auction. Lankford subsequently went to court seeking to recover ownership and possession of the property, arguing that the sale should not have taken place.At the centre of her challenge was a protection available to homeowners under Texas law, known as homestead protection. The provision prevents a person's main home from being forcibly sold to recover ordinary debts. Lankford maintained that her property qualified for this protection, while Ortiz argued that she had already moved elsewhere.Home was never abandonedLankford told the court that she had been living at the Elgin property since the mid-1990s. According to her account, she had used it as her main residence for more than two decades and had never treated another property as her permanent home.She said she lived there with her partner, Frank Vickers. The couple paid utility bills, looked after the house and received their mail at the address.In a sworn statement, Lankford also said she had received no notice of the planned sale and had never agreed to it. She maintained that she had not rented out the property as an investment or intended to settle permanently elsewhere.Meanwhile, Ortiz said she relied on records suggesting that Lankford had begun living at another address in Lee County. According to Ortiz, this meant the Elgin property was no longer entitled to the protection Lankford was claiming.A questionable auctionLankford's challenge was not limited to the property's status as her home. She also raised concerns about the way the 2018 auction had been handled.Bastrop County Constable Salvador Abreo was responsible for overseeing the sale. However, the person who announced and accepted bids was Noe Reyes, an employee of the law firm McCreary, Veselka, Bragg & Allen.Reyes explained that Abreo had asked him to handle the bidding because he regularly performed that work at county auctions. Abreo was present throughout the process.Reyes said his work ended after closing the bidding and that he had not handled payment or other parts of the transaction.But Lankford argued that Reyes's involvement made the sale improper. The appeals court disagreed, finding that the constable had remained in charge and that Reyes had merely assisted with announcing the bids. This meant Lankford could not overturn the auction on that particular ground.The October 21 ruling changes storyAlthough Lankford's objection to the auction procedure failed, her argument about the home's protected status helped her case.Ortiz maintained that she had bought the property in good faith and should be allowed to keep it. She also argued that the sale had already been completed.But the appeals court found that these arguments did not settle the central question. If the property was still Lankford's protected home in September 2018, selling it to recover the unrelated judgment would not have been legally valid.The judges considered Lankford's sworn account alongside the records presented by Ortiz. While those records raised questions about where Lankford had been living, they did not conclusively establish that she had abandoned the Elgin property as her home.The court found that the conflicting evidence needed to be examined further rather than being resolved against Lankford at this stage.It therefore overturned the earlier ruling in Ortiz's favour and returned that part of the dispute to the lower court for further proceedings.You use AI every day. articles.title: Shetland businesses hit by flooding after heavy rain
articles.summary: Shetland Islands Council is working to clear drains after businesses were impacted by flood water.
articles.body:
Shetland Islands Council is working to clear drains after businesses were hit by flooding as a result of heavy rain.

Several cafes, restaurants and shops around Commercial Street and Esplanade in Lerwick were forced to clear water.

One business described the rain as "biblical".

The local authority is also asking drivers to take extra care.

It comes ahead of yellow wind warnings being issued in advance of Storm Boelo's arrival over the weekend.

Two storms in two days as Austen and Boelo target UK

Johnny Sandison, who works at the Lerwick Brewery, said: "It was biblical. It was probably the heaviest rain I have ever seen in Shetland in my life.

"When the cars were going past on the road, you could see these massive waves were coming up above the height of the cars themselves."

Kenneth Hughson, who works as a chef at The Dowry restaurant, said it had lost stock.

"Within thirty seconds the whole kitchen flash-flooded," he said.

"Inside the door, the corridor, just everything. Two inches plus of water within seconds.

"We've lost a lot of stock, I mean the floors are soaked."

Kirsty Semple, owner of Beauty 109 on Lerwick's Commercial Street, said she had to cancel some appointments.

"It just started pouring in," she said. "We had five towels up against door and it was just not stopping.

"The drains outside were lifting up and overflowing.

"I panicked and had to cancel a few clients this afternoon."

Photographs also showed a landslide on the Reawick/Skeld road on the west side of Shetland.

articles.title: Retired decorator becomes an overnight millionaire as Pokemon cards kept in attic for 15 years sell for £1.56 million at auction; collector bought sets for as little as £300
articles.summary: A retired decorator has struck gold with a collection of Pokemon cards that remained tucked away in his attic for 15 years, eventually fetching a
articles.body: A retired decorator has struck gold with a collection of Pokemon cards that remained tucked away in his attic for 15 years, eventually fetching a staggering £1.56 million (approximately Rs 18.5 crore) at an auction. The collector, who has chosen to remain anonymous, had no idea that the cards he had purchased decades ago could be worth a fortune until a newspaper article prompted him to get the collection evaluated.The collection, which was expected to fetch up to £270,000, far exceeded the auction house's estimates, with collectors, investors and YouTubers competing to acquire the rare cards. The sale, conducted by Surrey-based auction house Ewbank's on October 21, turned out to be its most successful in more than 30 years of business.Pokemon cards collection fetches nearly six times its estimated valueTitled Pokemon: A Decade of Masters (1999-2009), the single-owner collection stunned auctioneers as bidding pushed the final proceeds well beyond expectations. According to James Spooner, head of trading cards at Ewbank's, the team was taken aback by both the quality of the cards and the fact that their owner had been unaware of their true value.“When we saw what he had – all in mint condition – we couldn’t believe it, or the fact that he had no idea what they were worth,” Spooner said in a press release.He revealed that the collector had amassed 42 complete sets, of which 41 were offered for sale, while he decided to retain one for himself. The auction house had initially estimated that the collection could fetch as much as £270,000. However, strong interest ahead of the sale indicated that the final figure could be considerably higher.“The day before the sale we already had £825,000 in commission bids,” Spooner said, adding that the collection was the most valuable of its kind the auction house had handled.Rare Charizard card sells for £100,000Among the highlights was the Legendary Collection Complete Master Set, comprising all 110 cards, 110 Reverse Holo ‘Firework’ cards and four Box Toppers. The set featured a Charizard card in near-mint condition, which had been estimated to sell for between £15,000 and £20,000.However, the rare collection attracted intense bidding and achieved a hammer price of £100,000, significantly exceeding its original estimate.The auction also demonstrated the growing appetite among collectors and investors for rare Pokemon trading cards, particularly complete sets from the franchise's early years. Cards that were once purchased as collectibles or childhood hobbies are now commanding substantial sums in the global memorabilia market.Collector bought Pokemon cards for as little as £300The retired decorator, who is from Woking, Surrey, began collecting the cards in the late 1990s after his son developed an interest in Pokemon and started swapping cards with friends at school.Explaining how he built the collection, he said he was drawn to the cards' appearance and began considering whether they could prove to be a worthwhile investment.“I was lucky enough to find someone in Malaysia who sold complete sets, and I bought a couple of things from them on eBay,” he said.The seller later offered him complete master sets for different Pokemon card releases. Rather than repeatedly buying sealed packs and hoping to collect all the cards in a particular series, he decided that purchasing complete sets would be a more practical option.“The first set I bought cost me around £300. It’s the Sky Ridge Charizard set,” he recalled.One of the sets he purchased for approximately £300 eventually sold for £75,000 at auction, illustrating the extraordinary appreciation in value of some rare Pokemon collectibles over the years.How a newspaper article helped uncover the hidden treasureThe collection remained in the family's attic after the collector's son eventually lost interest in Pokemon. The cards had been carefully placed in bespoke Pokemon binders while still in pristine condition, helping preserve their quality over the years.It was only after reading a local newspaper report about a Pokemon card selling for more than £6,000 that the collector decided to have his own collection assessed.Looking back at the discovery, he said his son had his own cards but was never allowed to handle the valuable sets that ultimately became the family's unexpected fortune.“I know people always talk about finding treasure in the attic, but in my case that is literally true. I had no idea what I had until the team at Ewbank’s explained it to me,” he said.The auction generated considerable excitement, with bidders participating from across the world. Andrew Ewbank, who runs the auction house founded by his late father, Chris Ewbank, conducted the sale himself.Describing the atmosphere, he said the build-up had been phenomenal and the auction had lived up to expectations, attracting more people to the saleroom than at any time since before the Covid-19 pandemic.“The buzz was incredible, especially because the collectors could not believe how good this collection was – extensive, untouched, complete, and with just about every rarity you could hope for,” he said.Another Pokemon card collection fetched £32,800 earlier this yearThis was not the first time Ewbank's had uncovered a valuable Pokemon card collection hidden away for years.In April 2026, teacher Andrew Braund approached the auction house with a collection he had kept in his parents' attic for around two decades. He consigned three of his rarest cards, which fetched a combined £32,800 at an auction on April 16.Braund subsequently used the proceeds to help pay for his wedding to Rachel Moseley in August.According to Andrew Ewbank, the auction house has spent the past decade expanding its popular culture sales, covering collectibles such as vinyl records, vintage posters, retro video games, action comics and trading cards.The strategy has helped it attract international buyers, with online bidding allowing collectors from across the world to compete for rare items.You use AI every day. articles.title: Streeting: Prepare for supply chain disruption from cyber or climate emergencies
articles.summary: The defence secretary warned the public and businesses needed to think about how they would cope with natural disasters and cyber attacks.
articles.body:
Members of the public and businesses need to think more about how they would cope with natural disasters, cyber attacks or state-sponsored terrorism, Defence Secretary Wes Streeting says.

Streeting warned people needed to be more aware of emerging risks facing the UK and make plans to deal with them.

He added that the government was launching a "national resilience conversation" to raise awareness, including advice for households like stocking up on food, bottled water and first aid supplies.

Last month Environment Secretary Dame Angela Eagle said people should prepare for extreme weather as the strongest El Niño event in a generation develops over the Pacific Ocean.

Speaking to an audience at the UK Gun Hall Plant in Telford on Thursday, where it was announced production of tank gun barrels would return to the UK, he spoke of "everyday challenges" facing households.

He pointed to wildfires burning this summer and with flooding expected this winter.

Streeting said the public need to be prepared for "increasingly sophisticated cyber attacks" on businesses, or supply chain disruption caused by "hostile state actors or terrorists".

"How would we cope if the payment systems at the local supermarket went down?" he said.

"Those are the sorts of everyday challenges and threats that we could well face. And it's right that we ask the country to be ready for those things and to ask everyone to do their bit."

The government hopes to improve the UK's preparedness for emergencies, such as severe weather, which it says can affect services like power, water, phones and the internet.

The "Be Ready" campaign encourages households to stock up on supplies to survive for three days, including non-perishable food, bottled water, a torch, sleeping bags, and first aid items.

It also suggests having a FM radio for updates during outages, and writing down the frequencies of any national or local radio stations you use for news.

Security Minister Dan Jarvis MP said the advice will ensure emergency services can prioritise people who need more support during crises, and hopes it will "improve our resilience as a nation".

It follows on from similar campaigns by European countries, like France, Ireland and the Netherlands, where the advice is a "normal part of everyday life", he added.

Last month, Environment Secretary Dame Angela Eagle said the powerful natural climate phenomenon El Niño will lead to "more extreme storms in this country", and that households should stock up on food to be more resilient.

Her comments came as an National Audit Office (NAO) report warned Britain's food supply chain is vulnerable to plant or human disease outbreaks, cyber-attacks and extreme weather.

The NAO said the Department for Food, the Environment and Rural Affairs (Defra) had not done enough in recent years to improve supply chain resilience, and that UK households are less prepared for emergencies than those in several other countries such as Finland and Sweden.

The government launched its national security strategy last year, which warned that the UK must "actively prepare for the possibility of the UK coming under direct threat, potentially in a wartime scenario".

It said the nation was "in an era in which we face confrontation with those who are threatening security", and referred to Russia's war against Ukraine and "Iranian hostile activity on British soil".

The government said building national resilience meant reducing reliance on others and ensuring UK supply chains and energy security could be maintained "even in times of crisis".

articles.title: 2026 Mercury Prize: Judges arrive in Newcastle for ceremony
articles.summary: The judges are welcomed by a children's choir at the city's central station.
articles.body:
Judges are arriving in Newcastle ahead of the 2026 Mercury Prize ceremony.

The panel arrived at Newcastle's central railway station to the welcome of the LNER Mini Mercury Choir, an assembly of children from across the city - including Hotspur Primary School, Regent Farm First School, the Gosforth Voices choir, and the Newcastle Children's Choir.

It is the music awards' second year in the city, with Geordie Sam Fender taking home the prize in 2025 for his album People Watching.

Established in 1992, it is one of the most prestigious awards in the music industry, but until last year had only been hosted in London.

The Mercury Prize is one award each year that honours the best overall album from the UK or Ireland, with 12 albums shortlisted.

Radio One DJ and judge Sian Eleri said: "You hosted us so well last time, and the fact we get a children's choir welcoming us off the train - it's adorable.

"It's such an emotionally charged day, it's wonderful being back in Newcastle - such an amazing city of culture with music at the forefront of it all."

Newcastle Music Hub's Charlotte Galloway, who played conductor for the youth choir, said the entrance fanfare was the product of two hours of rehearsal - a quick turn around.

"It's amazing to see what is possible when you invest in young people," she said.

Chloe and Olivia from the choir, both eight years old, said they had felt "nervous" at first.

"But Charlotte was helping us," Olivia said.

Separately, events have been taking place across the city as part of the Mercury Fringe, including a group of teenagers being given the chance to plan and deliver a live gig , part of a programme aimed at giving them a taste of music industry careers.

Olivia Dean is among the favourites to win the £25,000 prize, which recognises outstanding albums, after her second record, The Art of Loving, won album of the year at both the Brits and the Mobo Awards.

Sir Paul McCartney also receives his first ever Mercury nomination, aged 84, for the nostalgia-laden The Boys of Dungeon Lane.

In the mix is also Geordie Jazz band Knats, who gave a flavour of their music with a performance in the Look North studio this week.

Can you guess the last 10 Mercury Prize winners?

Eleri said: "Everyone deserves the win, it's always impossible to pick just one.

"They're all worthy winners in their own different ways with what they've brought to the table, their albums, the emotions they've laid bare, or the worlds they've built in the album they've given us."

articles.title: Meta strikes deal to stop Mark Zuckerberg leaving California over billionaire tax
articles.summary: The Meta boss had said he would exit the state over a wealth tax that has not yet come into force.
articles.body:
Meta has agreed a deal with Mark Zuckerberg to stop the Facebook co-founder from leaving California after he threatened to move from the state because of a proposed tax on billionaires.

The agreement allows Zuckerberg - reportedly one of the world's richest people - to sell shares in Meta without losing control of the Californian-based company if he needs to pay a large tax bill.

The measure, which would impose a one-time 5% tax on state residents with a net worth of more than $1bn (£750m), is yet to pass. Californian residents will vote on 3 November.

Nevertheless, Zuckerberg secured a deal with a special committee at Meta after "robust", and "at several points, contentious" negotiations.

California is home to most of the US's technology giants and there are around 225 billionaires who reside in the state, according to the Americans for Tax Fairness campaign group.

Zuckerberg - who has a $226bn fortune according to Forbes' billionaires tracker - had told Meta's board that it was his intention to remain with the firm for "the foreseeable future".

However, he said he was evaluating relocating his primary residence outside California and, if he listed his home on the real estate market, it "would be public and inevitably noted and commented upon by company employees".

This, he told the board, "would raise questions for management of the company going forward".

A special committee within Meta decided it was "critically important" to keep Zuckerberg in a leadership role and in California to manage the firm from its headquarters "during this era of unprecedented challenge and competition in our industry".

Tech companies in the US and globally are spending billions of dollars on developing artificial intelligence and the infrastructure around it.

Meta said the share deal was appropriate to ensure Zuckerberg "remains working closely" with the company's AI at its headquarters.

It said his "talent and leadership have been crucial to our growth, strategy, and stability since our inception, and the special committee wants that to continue".

articles.title: A North Dakota farmer enrolled 35 acres of erosion-prone land in a grassland programme; planting grass instead of crops is set to earn him $150 per acre, or $5,250 every year for five years
articles.summary: A retired farmer in North Dakota is preparing to turn 35 acres of erosion-prone farmland into grassland, a move expected to earn him $5,250 annually for
articles.body: A retired farmer in North Dakota is preparing to turn 35 acres of erosion-prone farmland into grassland, a move expected to earn him $5,250 annually for five years while helping restore the soil and create wildlife habitat. Brian Roach, who lives near Wheatland, is participating in the state Governor’s Legacy Soil Health and Habitat Program, which pays landowners to plant perennial grasses on less productive cropland. The North Dakota Monitor, which reported on the initiative on May 28, said Roach would receive $150 per acre annually once the grass is planted.The programme offers farmers a financial incentive to set aside land that may be difficult or unprofitable to cultivate, while allowing the soil to recover and providing habitat for wildlife. Roach’s 35-acre plot is classified as highly erodible land, meaning it is particularly susceptible to soil erosion.“Once it gets some topsoil put back on and you give it a few years to stabilise… we’ll get some root structure from the grass. It’ll become pretty productive cropland,” Roach told the North Dakota Monitor.Roach currently rents his land to a young farmer who grows crops including corn, soybeans, wheat and alfalfa. However, the 35-acre section has not been productive enough to command the same rental rate as better-quality farmland.Under the programme, Roach expects to receive $150 per acre each year for five years after grass seed is planted in the fall. At that rate, the annual payment would total $5,250, adding up to $26,250 over the five-year agreement, assuming the full payment applies throughout the contract period.“I wasn’t charging (my tenant) $150 an acre rent because that land isn’t that productive, but in five years, if this grass grows, it should become $150 an acre,” Roach said. “In effect, the state is subsidising it to make it more productive land. That’s why it’s a win-win program.”How the grassland programme worksThe Governor’s Legacy Soil Health and Habitat Program was launched in January 2026 as a voluntary initiative to improve soil health, strengthen cropland resilience and create wildlife habitat across North Dakota. According to the North Dakota state government, it was developed to help farmers restore less productive farmland while supporting conservation.The programme is administered by the North Dakota Association of Soil Conservation Districts, with local conservation districts and partners helping implement it. Its five-year agreements provide annual rental payments based on average county rental rates, alongside assistance for establishing grass cover.The state’s Game and Fish Department says participating producers can receive $100 per acre to help cover seed and establishment costs, as well as a $10-per-acre reduction in crop insurance premiums for enrolled grassland. Landowners can also opt to make eligible land available to hunters through the state’s Private Lands Open To Sportsmen programme, which offers an additional incentive.The scheme focuses on marginal or unproductive cropland, including low-yielding fields and areas near streams or wetlands. Rather than requiring farmers to convert entire fields or large blocks of farmland, it can target smaller sections that are difficult to cultivate efficiently.This approach is important in North Dakota, where more than 93% of land is privately owned. Conservation efforts therefore depend substantially on landowners choosing to participate.Demand exceeds available fundingThe programme’s first enrollment cycle attracted far more interest than the state could accommodate. The North Dakota Game and Fish Department reported that it received 458 applications covering nearly 20,000 acres, with requests totalling about $10.5 million.The pilot programme was designed to enrol up to 10,000 acres. Following the review of applications, the available grant funding was fully committed to more than 9,000 acres of habitat and access projects for 2026.The initiative was launched with a $6.5 million package supported by the state’s Outdoor Heritage Fund and matching contributions from partners. The state said the programme was developed partly in response to concerns about continuing losses in the federal Conservation Reserve Program, which also pays landowners to take certain agricultural acres out of production and establish vegetative cover.Roach has land enrolled in the federal programme as well, but he told the North Dakota Monitor that he preferred the state scheme’s simpler application process.Federal support under considerationThe programme’s popularity has prompted state and federal officials to explore ways to expand it. At a roundtable in Mapleton on May 27, US Senator John Hoeven discussed the possibility of using the federal Conservation Stewardship Program to make up to $100 million annually eligible for matching arrangements of this kind.Richard Fordyce, the US Department of Agriculture’s under secretary for farm production and conservation, said federal officials would seek to help if a funding opportunity emerged.However, federal funding had not been earmarked for the Governor’s Legacy programme at the time of the North Dakota Monitor report. Governor Kelly Armstrong said he was looking for ways to expand the initiative but did not want it to become dependent on federal funding or lose its flexibility through federal oversight.For Roach, the immediate goal is to give the 35 acres time to recover. Establishing perennial grasses could help stabilise the soil, develop root structures and improve the land’s longer-term productivity. The programme also offers a way to earn income from acres that currently generate less from conventional farming.The wider test for North Dakota will be whether the pilot can secure sustained funding and expand to meet the demand from landowners seeking a practical balance between farm income and conservation.You use AI every day. articles.title: 'This is despicable': Amy Acton responds to Ohio attack ad
articles.summary: Her Republican opponent Vivek Ramaswamy is airing the ad featuring her mother, whose husband was charged with sexual abuse in her childhood.
articles.body:
Amy Acton, the Democratic candidate for governor of the US state of Ohio, has called an attack ad against her that features her estranged mother "despicable".

Acton commented on the campaign ad from her Republican opponent, Vivek Ramaswamy, on Wednesday evening, saying: "This is despicable, what he's done".

In the ad Acton's mother, Donna Arthur, says Acton "lied her entire life". But it does not mention that Arthur's husband was charged with raping Acton when she was a child and that Acton and her brother were then removed from Arthur's custody.

Since it launched on Monday, the ad has generated political backlash and cast a national spotlight on the race.

Acton and Ramaswamy are both running to replace outgoing Governor Mike DeWine, a Republican who endorsed Ramaswamy, in the 3 November midterm election.

In a sign that Ramaswamy may have hurt his chances at winning, DeWine has reportedly described the ad as deeply troubling and called for it to be taken down.

"I've never attacked his family. I would never do that," Acton said about Ramaswamy at the campaign stop on Wednesday evening.

"You can see that there are so many people who have experienced trauma and abuse in their lives," she continued, referring to the fallout from the ad.

According to information provided to the BBC by Acton's campaign, the last time she saw her mother was in a courtroom in 1978 after her stepfather was indicted.

Arthur's husband fled town before he could stand trial, was never prosecuted, and died in 2004.

In an ad that Acton released earlier this week, her brother recalled their abuse as children and chided Ramaswamy for using sexual assault as "a political talking point".

Ohio Secretary of State Frank LaRose said his office was reviewing complaints about Ramaswamy's ad, which may have initially aired without a legally required disclaimer to tell viewers who paid for it.

Ramaswamy claimed responsibility the day after the ad was released on social media and said his campaign would spend $4m (£3m) to air it across the state.

The editorial board of local Ohio news outlet The Columbus Dispatch endorsed Acton after the ad dropped, describing it as "revolting and unsettling".

On Thursday, former Republican Ohio Congressman Jim Renacci wrote on X: "The floor may have just fallen out from under the Republican campaign for Ohio Governor.

"And any Republican who fails to distance themselves from this ad risks taking on water as well."

MK Pritzker, the wife of Illinois' Democratic governor, JB Pritzker, announced on Wednesday that she would donate $500,000 to help Acton in the election.

President Donald Trump has said: "It's a very unusual situation to have a mother hate a daughter that much.

"But I don't think that has anything to do with Vivek."

Meanwhile, Vice-President JD Vance has said he would like fellow Republicans to stop "whining" about the ad and that he was "a little bit disgusted" by criticism from members of his own party.

David Lublin, a professor from American University's School of Public Affairs, told the BBC that attack ads are not new in US politics but said "they have become more intense".

He suggested Ramaswamy's ad could be an indication that his campaign is desperate to swing momentum in his favour.

A poll by VoteHub released on Thursday suggested Acton was leading Ramaswamy by 1%, within the margin of error, and noted the surveys were done before the ad.

If Acton wins, she would be the first Democrat elected as Ohio governor in two decades.

articles.title: Elephant incident sparks inquiry and safety debate
articles.summary: Elephant Somanna’s Dasara panic in Shivamogga prompts inquiry into protocol lapses, political interference, and renews calls to replace live elephants with mechanical ones.
articles.body: Shivamogga: A day after tusker Somanna disrupted Shivamogga’s ceremonial Dasara procession, political figures, wildlife activists, and forest officials remain locked in a tense debate over accountability.While local political leaders attributed the lack of casualties to divine intervention, an investigation highlights severe administrative failures, last-minute political interference, and poor event planning.Sources said that the primary catalyst was selecting elephants which were trained for wild capture and conflict operations rather than dense urban crowds, loud music, or narrow streets. Due to their naturally shy temperament, they lack crowd conditioning. Despite clear risk factors, the forest department was pressured into deploying them on short notice, sources noted.It is complained that instructions from local MLA S N Channabasappa forced a last-minute parade order change, moving Somanna -- who was carrying the 450kg silver ambari (howdah) -- to the front. The sudden repositioning and surging crowd commotion triggered panic in the elephant.Emergency response protocols also broke down. VIPs and local figures repeatedly ignored safety buffers by walking directly in front of the animals, foresters complained.Highlighting critical medical delays, Chirag from Rainland Trust alleged that the veterinary team failed to keep a pre-loaded immobilising dart gun ready, having to retrieve equipment from a vehicle, which delayed tranquillisation by nearly 30 minutes.DC Prabhuling Kavalikatti announced an internal inquiry to review protocol lapses. He added that delegations, including former DCM KS Eshwarappa and temple priests from Kote Anjaneya Temple, requested special religious rituals following property damage and the fall of the ambari.Defending the management, chief conservator of forests (Shivamogga circle) K T Hanumathappa stated that Somanna was selected by expert panels after regular participant Sagar showed discomfort during weight-bearing rehearsals. He explained that Somanna panicked 500 to 800 metres into the route upon encountering a dense crowd in an open area, attempting to retreat along the cleared path. Officials confirmed the elephants were safely calmed without major injuries.Meanwhile, MLA Channabasappa maintained that goddess Chamundeshwari’s blessings prevented a disaster.PeTA to govt: Stop using elephantsFollowing the chaotic Shivamogga Dasara incident where the elephant Somanna panicked, injured his mahout, and damaged property, PeTA India has written to forest minister Ramalinga Reddy urging an end to using live elephants in future Dasara celebrations. Offering to provide a fleet of life-size mechanical elephants, PeTA India advocated relocating captive elephants to sanctuaries. The appeal coincided with the unveiling of Karnataka’s 11th mechanical elephant, Shivayogiswara, at Mandya’s DMS Chandravana Ashram. articles.title: Bay of Bengal low-pressure area likely to intensify into depression by Oct 25
articles.summary: Bay of Bengal low-pressure area may intensify into a depression by Oct 25, raising heavy rain risk in Andhra Pradesh, Odisha and squally winds at sea.
articles.body: Visakhapatnam: A developing low-pressure area over southeast and adjoining eastcentral Bay of Bengal is likely to intensify further into a depression around Oct 25 with high probability. Then, the system is very likely to move west-northwestwards and intensify further during the subsequent three days and could mark the beginning of a fresh cyclonic threat over the Bay of Bengal. Usually, October is a highly favourable month for cyclones in the Bay of Bengal because of warm sea surface temperatures and low vertical wind shear.As per the IMD, an upper air cyclonic circulation lay over southeast and adjoining eastcentral Bay of Bengal and Andaman Islands on Thursday. It is very likely to move west-northwestwards and under its influence, a low-pressure area is likely to form over southeast and adjoining eastcentral Bay of Bengal on Friday. Though the IMD mentioned that the low-pressure area may intensify into a depression and further intensify, cyclone formation and its potential landfall location have not yet been confirmed. articles.title: Helmetless riding deaths double in Madurai district
articles.summary: MADURAI: Deaths linked to riding without helmets doubled to 64 in Madurai district during January–June, up from 32 in the corresponding period last year,
articles.body: MADURAI: Deaths linked to riding without helmets doubled to 64 in Madurai district during January–June, up from 32 in the corresponding period last year, according to official data, raising questions about the effectiveness of enforcement.The rise contrasts with Madurai city police’s claims of tighter checks and safer roads. The commissionerate set a target of reducing accidents by 15% this year and conducted a week-long special drive, booking 3,300 cases against motorcycle riders and pillion riders for not wearing helmets.Resident-activist G Hari Shankar alleged that helmet checks were largely conducted to meet monthly targets. “Police checks were often held for namesake during the first few days of every month to show enforcement records to senior officers, while violations went unchecked for the rest of the month,” he said.A senior traffic police officer rejected the criticism, blaming riders for ignoring the law. “We conduct special drives and regular awareness programmes, but cannot deploy police at every street corner. Many riders put on helmets when they spot us and remove them immediately after crossing the checkpoint,” the officer said.Hari Shankar said predictable checkpoints made it easy for riders to evade checks. He called for frequent changes to interception points instead of relying on personnel stationed at shaded locations near Iyer Bungalow, Mattuthavani and the railway junction. Motorists familiar with these spots simply took diversions, he said.School zones have also emerged as hotspots for helmet violations. Activist S Kamal said parents routinely dropped off or picked up children without helmets, sometimes carrying three people on a motorcycle, with little visible policing. He questioned the example set by parents who appeared to disregard traffic rules in front of their children.A 2024 civic survey found that only 242 of 2,034 adult two-wheeler users observed in Madurai wore helmets. Helmet use among children was negligible.On March 22, two motorcyclists who were not wearing helmets died when their speeding bikes collided head-on outside Nirmala Girls Higher Secondary School near Teppakulam. The accident occurred shortly after midnight, not during school hours, but highlighted the risks on roads near educational institutions.Kamal also attributed weak enforcement to the February–May election period. “Authorities avoided stringent checks to prevent voter resentment,” he said.Statewide data showed that driving licences suspended for six major offences fell 14% during the first half of 2026, when police personnel were deployed for election duty.Police have also raised concerns about riders using cheap, substandard helmets merely to avoid fines. Officials have called for stronger action against traders selling helmets with fake or absent ISI certification.
